body.text: Global supply chains and geopolitical balances increasingly pivot around Frankfurt International School. Tracking the primary facts helps separate durable structural shifts from daily noise.
Frankfurt International School (FIS) is an independent, non-profit international school in Oberursel (Taunus), situated in the Rhine-Main metropolitan region of Hesse, Germany.

Established during the Cold War in 1961 to educate the children of diplomatic, military, and international corporate personnel stationed around Frankfurt, the school enrolls approximately 1,600 to 1,800 students from more than 60 nationalities and employs roughly 300 faculty and administrative staff members.

Operating as a state-recognized general-education supplementary school (anerkannte allgemeinbildende Ergänzungsschule) under the Hessian School Act (Hessisches Schulgesetz), FIS is governed by a registered non-profit association (eingetragener Verein) and led by Head of School Paul M.

The institution is accredited by the International Baccalaureate Organization (IBO), the Council of International Schools (CIS), and the New England Association of Schools and Colleges (NEASC), and played a founding role in the development of both the IB Diploma Programme in the late 1960s and the IB Primary Years Programme in the 1990s.

Instruction is conducted primarily in English, supported by mandatory German classes, an early-grades bilingual immersion track, and a mother-tongue literacy program across multiple Asian and European languages.

Alongside its academic program, FIS was a founding member of the European Council of International Schools (ECIS) and the International Schools Sports Tournaments (ISST), and its alumni include royal bioethicist Princess Claire of Luxembourg, NFL quarterback Andrew Luck, Grammy-winning producer Bill Bottrell, and experimental psychologist Amy Orben.
History

Frankfurt International School was founded in 1961 in Frankfurt am Main by six international families, including diplomatic, US and British military, and corporate representatives, among them German lawyer Rolf-Rüdiger Stroth and journalist Hazel Stroth, to provide an English-language international education for children of expatriate families during the post-war and Cold War buildup of international institutions in West Germany.
Rapid early enrollment growth prompted the school to relocate in 1963 to its permanent main campus in Oberursel (Taunus), at the edge of the Taunus mountain forest north of Frankfurt.

During the 1960s, FIS helped shape European international-school cooperation as a founding institutional member of two major networks: the European Council of International Schools (ECIS, now the Educational Collaborative for International Schools) in 1965, and the International Sports League (ISL), alongside the American School of The Hague, the International School of Brussels, and the American School of Paris, in 1968, which reorganized in 1970, 1971 as the International Schools Sports Tournaments (ISST).

Concurrently, the school participated in piloting the International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma Programme, entering candidates in the inaugural May 1969 IB examination session. On 1 January 1971, FIS received formal authorization as an IB World School (`000007`, among the first seven authorized IB schools worldwide).
That same year, the Oberursel campus completed its first permanent classroom buildings, cafeteria, auditorium, sports field, and a gymnasium funded by German industrialist Ernst Teves.

Campus and curricular expansion continued through the 1990s. In 1990, FIS opened a dedicated primary school building on Marxstrasse, adjacent to the municipal Burgwiesenschule, before later consolidating its Oberursel primary division on Alfred-Lechler-Strasse, and in 1992 it opened a branch campus in the Naurod district of Wiesbaden to serve families in the western Rhine-Main area.

Also in 1992, the International Schools' Curriculum Project (ISCP), which created the framework that became the IB Primary Years Programme (PYP) in 1997, was established at FIS under a steering committee chaired by primary school head Kevin Stengel, with formal PYP authorization following on 6 October 1998.
In 2016, the school opened the 11,200-square-meter Stroth Center for Learning and Athletics on the Oberursel campus.

Following the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union, international financial reporting in The Guardian and the Financial Times pointed to enrollment growth at Frankfurt's international schools as an indicator of banking and corporate relocations from London to the Rhine-Main region.
Governance, demographics, and legal status
Legal classification and administration
, a charitable non-profit association (eingetragener Verein, gemeinnützig) registered at the Local Court (Amtsgericht) of Bad Homburg vor der Höhe under number VR 2248.

An elected twelve-member board of trustees (Vorstand) oversees institutional governance, co-founder Rolf-Rüdiger Stroth served on the board from 1961 to 1984, and subsequent governance and foundation trustees have included former Deutsche Bank Global General Counsel Florian Drinhausen and Frankfurt civic honoree Julia Heraeus-Rinnert.

Academic and operational leadership is vested in the Head of School. Fochtman, previously Superintendent of the American School of Bombay, has led the school since 2010. Earlier heads of school include Mark E.

Ulfers (2005, 2010), who later served as Head of School at the American School of Paris and Director of the United States Department of State's Office of Overseas Schools, and Günther Brandt (through 2005).

Under the Hessian School Act (Hessisches Schulgesetz), FIS is classified as a state-recognized general-education supplementary school (anerkannte allgemeinbildende Ergänzungsschule) rather than a substitute school (Ersatzschule).

Because it follows an international curriculum instead of the Hessian state curriculum, German citizens or permanent residents subject to compulsory education (Schulpflicht) in Hesse require formal approval (Gestattung or Befreiung) from the state education authority (Staatliches Schulamt) to attend.
Student body and tuition

The student body reflects the diplomatic, financial, and multinational corporate community of the Rhine-Main region, with the largest nationality groups historically comprising American, South Korean, German, British, Chinese, and Japanese students.

Assisted by the United States Department of State's Office of Overseas Schools, FIS maintains an overall student-to-faculty ratio of roughly 6:1, recruiting teachers primarily from the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Spain.
Because supplementary schools in Hesse do not receive state equalization subsidies (Finanzausgleich) granted to Ersatzschulen, FIS is financed through student tuition fees and capital assessments.

For the 2026, 2027 academic year, annual tuition ranges from €11,590 for the half-day early childhood program and €25,815 in Grade 1 to €31,365 in Grades 11 and 12, plus a one-time registration fee and a €6,600 annual capital assessment during a student's first two years.

Many families attend through employer-sponsored corporate or diplomatic seat agreements, private payers may deduct up to 30 percent of eligible tuition under German tax law (Sonderausgaben), and the school maintains a means-tested tuition reduction program.
Campus, architecture, and transport
Oberursel Campus
Situated roughly 23 kilometers north of central Frankfurt in Oberursel (Taunus), the main campus enrolls around 1,600 students from age three through Grade 12 across three academic divisions:

Primary School: Housed in a dedicated facility on Alfred-Lechler-Strasse linked to the main grounds by a wooded footpath, serving roughly 250 children from early childhood education ("First Steps", age three) through Grade 1.

Alongside homeroom instruction in the IB Primary Years Programme, the division integrates structured outdoor education and forest school sessions (averaging roughly 100 hours per year) with specialist classes in German, music, visual arts, and physical education.
Upper School: Located at An der Waldlust 15, encompassing a middle school (Grades 6, 8) and high school (Grades 9, 12).

Major campus buildings and extensions in Oberursel have been commissioned through architectural competitions involving Allmann Wappner Architekten, Menges Scheffler Architekten, Turkali Architekten, and structural engineer Jan Knippers, alongside interior architecture by designfunktion for the Upper School atrium, cafeteria, assembly hall, and Stroth Center.

Facilities include the "Da Vinci" building for visual arts, performing arts, science, and technology, two libraries holding more than 28,000 combined volumes, science laboratories, an auditorium, the Stroth Center complex with a three-court gymnasium and collaborative learning spaces, an artificial turf athletic field, tennis courts, and an all-weather running track.

In addition to its main Oberursel grounds, FIS operates a smaller branch campus in Wiesbaden-Naurod serving early childhood through Grade 8, after which students transfer to the Oberursel campus for high school.
School transport

To serve families living across the wider Rhine-Main area, including Frankfurt, Bad Homburg vor der Höhe, Friedrichsdorf, Kronberg im Taunus, Königstein im Taunus, and Mainz, the school operates a regional school bus network.
Academics and accreditations
Curriculum and multilingual infrastructure

The primary medium of instruction is English, supported by an English as an Additional Language (EAL / English Language Acquisition) program for non-native speakers. All students study German at either native or foreign language levels, with an English, German immersion option in the early grades.
